title: Mourning as devotion
hookLine: in Muharram many Shia communities hold majalis, recite elegies and serve water

lines: A HALL WITH THE LIGHTS LOW.
A CHANT, AND THE ROOM ANSWERS.
cards: A hall with the lights turned low. Black cloth on the walls. People sit on the floor, shoulder to shoulder, and someone at the front begins to speak about a camp by a river.
Halfway through, a voice rises into a chant, and the room answers. Some beat their chests in rhythm. Some cover their faces.

By the door, a table with jugs of water and cups for anyone walking past. This is a majlis in Muharram, and in Shia communities it can happen night after night. To an outsider it can look like grief that will not end.
Shia teachers call it something closer to love. Today: mourning as devotion.

teach.b: A majlis is simply a sitting, a gathering. In Muharram it becomes a gathering to remember Husayn. A speaker retells Karbala, often one person or one moment each night: the thirst, al-Abbas at the river, Zaynab's voice.
Then come the elegies, poems of grief sung or chanted, and the room weeps. Why weep for someone who died so long ago? Shia teachers answer: because we love him, and because the Prophet ﷺ loved him.
Tears for Husayn are tears for the Prophet's own grandson, a way of standing with the Prophet's family. The weeping is the point, not a side effect. Tears themselves have a place in Islam.
When the Prophet's infant son Ibrahim was dying, the hadith says, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears. Someone was surprised.

teach.h: THE EYE WEEPS, THE HEART GRIEVES.
teach.b: He said, in effect: the eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. Grief is not a failure of faith.
The Qur'an gives the words believers say when loss arrives: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Mourning held like this faces God rather than turning away. Then the water.
Because the camp at Karbala was kept from the river, Shia communities in Muharram set out water for strangers. A cup handed to someone you'll never see again becomes a small act of remembrance.

how: In Muharram, Shia communities hold majalis, gatherings where a speaker retells Karbala and reciters chant elegies, and some set out water and food for passersby in Husayn's memory.

a gathering, in Muharram, to remember Husayn

s: in Islam, weeping at a death shows weak faith
the hadith says the Prophet's eyes filled with tears when his son Ibrahim was dying.
a majlis in Muharram retells Karbala and ends in elegies
a speaker tells the story, then poems of grief are chanted and the room weeps.
the water set out in Muharram is just hospitality, with no link to Karbala
it remembers the camp that was kept from the river.

games.q: the Prophet's infant son is dying. someone expects him to hold back his tears. what does he do?
o: he hides his face so no one sees.
he weeps, and says the heart grieves but we say only what pleases our Lord.
he leaves the room until it is over.
games.why: the hadith says his eyes filled with tears, and he explained that grief and faith can sit together.

practice: Bring to mind someone you have lost, or someone you love who is far away, and let the grief be there without hurrying it off. Notice whose face comes with it.
If you pray, ask God's mercy for that person in your own words; if you don't, simply stay with them for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Majlis, a sitting, a gathering: in Muharram, the gathering where Shia Muslims retell Karbala, weep for Husayn, and set out water, offering grief itself as love. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a sitting or gathering; in Muharram, a gathering to remember Husayn.

carryVoice: Your line: grief as love. Tears can be a way of staying close. See you tomorrow.
